title: Weyl transport completes partial root maps and rank-one centralizer maps
statement: Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $P=(G,T=D_A(M),\Phi,\Phi^\vee,\Delta,(X_\alpha))$ a pinned split realization [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Use the root subgroups $U_\gamma$, exponentials $\exp_\gamma$, Weyl representatives $n_\alpha$, reflections $s_\alpha$, orders $m_{\alpha\beta}$, torus elements $t_{\alpha\beta}$ and positive two-root subgroups $U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$ of [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. An affine $A$-group scheme is an affine scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams; all homomorphisms below preserve those operations. Let $H$ be such a group. Let $N=N_G(T)$ denote the normalizer subgroup scheme: its points normalize $T$ after every further algebra extension. For $\alpha\in\Delta$, put $L_\alpha=M\cap\mathbf Q\alpha$ and $S_\alpha=D_A(M/L_\alpha)\subseteq T$, and let $K_\alpha=Z_G(S_\alpha)$ denote the rank-one centralizer subgroup scheme; its points commute with $S_\alpha$ after every further algebra extension. Give a homomorphism $f_N:N\to H$, and write $f_T=f_N|_T$ and $h_\alpha=f_N(n_\alpha)$. Give homomorphisms $f_\alpha:U_\alpha\to H$ for simple $\alpha$, and, for each unordered pair of distinct simple roots, $q_{\alpha\beta}:U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}\to H$ restricting to $f_\alpha,f_\beta$. Assume, on every commutative $A$-algebra $R$, $$f_T(t)f_\alpha(u)f_T(t)^{-1}=f_\alpha(tut^{-1}),\qquad (h_\alpha f_\alpha(\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)))^3=1,$$ for $t\in T(R),u\in U_\alpha(R)$, and $$h_\alpha q_{\alpha\beta}(v)h_\alpha^{-1}=q_{\alpha\beta}(n_\alpha v n_\alpha^{-1})\quad(v\in U_c(R),\ c\in\Psi_{\alpha\beta}\setminus\{\alpha\}),$$ together with the analogous equation with $\alpha,\beta$ interchanged. Then there are homomorphisms $g_\gamma:U_\gamma\to H$ for every $\gamma\in\Phi$ and $F_\alpha:K_\alpha\to H$ for every simple $\alpha$, with the following properties. One has $g_\alpha=f_\alpha$ on simple roots and $g_c=q_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_c}$ for every $c\in\Psi_{\alpha\beta}$. For all $A$-algebras $R$, $n\in N(R)$ with Weyl image $w$, and $u\in U_\gamma(R)$, $$f_N(n)g_\gamma(u)f_N(n)^{-1}=g_{w\gamma}(nun^{-1}).$$ This is interpreted on open-and-closed parts of $\operatorname{Spec}R$ when $w$ is locally constant. The map $F_\alpha$ restricts to $g_\alpha,g_{-\alpha}$ on the opposite root groups and to $f_N$ on $N\cap K_\alpha$. Moreover, for each root $\gamma$ there exist a simple root $\beta$ and a word in the $n_\alpha$ whose Weyl image carries $\beta$ to $\gamma$. For any word $n=n_{\alpha_1}\cdots n_{\alpha_k}$ represents $w$ and $w\beta=\gamma$ with $\beta$ simple, then $$g_\gamma(u)=f_N(n)f_\beta(n^{-1}un)f_N(n)^{-1};$$ this formula is independent of $\beta$ and the word. There is no Noetherian, reducedness, connectedness or residue-characteristic assumption.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed pp.202–203: Weyl-word construction of all-root maps, its Tits root-system compatibility input, and the rank-one centralizer calculation. Read Conrad online; local archival PDF WANTED. This node states the omitted compatibility argument as a separate obligation; no other source is invoked. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text: For a normalizer lift $r$ of $w\in W$ and a simple root $b$, define the candidate on $U_{wb}$ by $C(r,b)(u)=f_N(r)f_b(r^{-1}ur)f_N(r)^{-1}$. These are homomorphisms of affine group schemes by the conjugation isomorphisms in [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. They are $T$-equivariant: insert $r^{-1}tr\in T(R)$ into the assumed equivariance for $f_b$ and use that $f_N$ is a homomorphism. Replacing $r$ by $rt$, for $t\in T(R)$, changes the inner argument by $t^{-1}(-)t$ and the outer conjugator by $f_T(t)$, so the two changes cancel. Thus the candidate depends only on $(w,b)$, even for nonconstant torus points over an arbitrary test algebra.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: candidate transport formula and torus ambiguity.

proof.text: Fix $a\ne b$ and put $q=q_{ab}$. For $c\in\Psi_{ab}$, choose $e\in\{a,b\}$ and a positive path $e_i=s_{j_i}e_{i-1}$ from [lem-sfb-root-marked-parabolic-connectivity], ending at $c$. Start with $q|_{U_e}=f_e$. At the $i$th step the hypothesis applies because $e_{i-1}\ne j_i$ and both roots remain in $\Psi_{ab}$, and gives $q|_{U_{e_i}}=\operatorname{Int}(h_{j_i})\circ(q|_{U_{e_{i-1}}})\circ\operatorname{Int}(n_{j_i}^{-1})$. Substitution for $i=1,\ldots,k$ gives $q|_{U_c}=C(n_{j_k}\cdots n_{j_1},e)$. This also proves $T$-equivariance of each restriction by step 1. For any $v\in W_{ab}$ carrying $e$ to $c$, the same cited lemma gives a positive path representing that very $v$; consequently the formula holds for any normalizer lift of $v$, using step 1 to absorb its torus factor.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: dihedral compatibility from (6.2.5)--(6.2.6).

proof.text: If $(w,c)\sim(wv,e)$ is one generating move of [lem-sfb-root-marked-parabolic-connectivity], then $c,e\in\{a,b\}$ and $v(e)=c$. Step 2 says $f_c=C(r_v,e)$ for any lift $r_v$ of $v$. Conjugate this equality by a lift $r_w$ of $w$. The result is $C(r_w,c)=C(r_wr_v,e)$. Step 1 removes the choice of lift of $wv$. The cited connectivity theorem now equates the candidates for every two pairs with the same root, and its surjectivity supplies a pair for each root. Define $g_\gamma$ to be that common candidate. The pair $(1,\alpha)$ gives $g_\alpha=f_\alpha$, and step 2 gives $g_c=q_{ab}|_{U_c}$. Since $W$ is generated by the simple reflections, a chosen $w$ is represented by a word in the $s_\alpha$, whose lift is the corresponding word in the $n_\alpha$. This proves existence of the words and the asserted formula with independence of both the word and the simple root.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: root-system compatibility, explicitly applying the marked-root moves.

proof.text: Let $u\in U_\gamma(R)$ and write $\gamma=wb$ with $b$ simple and lift $r_w$. For a normalizer point $n$ with constant Weyl image $v$, the defining expression gives $f_N(n)g_\gamma(u)f_N(n)^{-1}=C(nr_w,b)(nun^{-1})=g_{v\gamma}(nun^{-1})$ by step 3. The quotient description in [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus] writes $N$ as the open-and-closed cosets represented by Weyl words. A locally constant Weyl image therefore gives a finite open-and-closed decomposition of $\operatorname{Spec}R$; the preceding equality on each part is the desired equality on $R$. On the zero test algebra all schemes have a unique point and the equality is automatic.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202, together with the normalizer equivariance needed in Theorem 6.2.1.

proof.text: Fix a simple $a$. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-root-rank-one-centralizer] to its root line: the primitive vector spanning $M\cap\mathbf Qa$ defines precisely $S_a$, and $K_a=Z_G(S_a)$ is reductive with torus $T$ and roots exactly $\{a,-a\}$. Its two root lines are the free ambient ones. Root exponentials, the coroot and the pinned representative agree with the ambient ones by [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus]. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-framed-noetherian-descent] to $K_a$ with generators of its two root lines, then [lem-sfb-relative-rank-one-local-matrix-model] to that Noetherian model. Pull back its affine-open cover to $A$. On this cover $(K_a,T)$ is a central split torus times one of the standard pairs SL2, PGL2 or GL2. Only the group and its framing are descended, not $H$ or any of the supplied maps. The pinning can be normalized in each matrix model by diagonal conjugation, since its positive root vector is a unit multiple of the standard one; uniqueness of the linked negative generator then fixes the negative coordinate as well.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: reduction to the three rank-one matrix pairs, with finite-presentation descent to remove the Noetherian restriction in the available matrix-model node.

proof.text: In these coordinates put $x'(z)=f_a(\exp_a(zX_a))$, $d'(t)=f_T(a^\vee(t))$ and $h=h_a$. The coroot acts on its root by $t^2$, so $d'(t)x'(z)d'(t)^{-1}=x'(t^2z)$. Since $f_N$ is a homomorphism and $n_a$ acts on $T$ by $s_a$, it gives $hd'(t)h^{-1}=d'(t^{-1})$ and $h^2=d'(-1)$. The remaining cubic identity is an assumption of the item. Thus [lem-sfb-sl2-cubic-gauss-identity] applies, with $y'(z)=h x'(-z)h^{-1}$. It supplies both Gauss interchange formulas on $1+uv$ invertible and $h=x'(1)y'(-1)x'(1)$. These are equalities over arbitrary algebras, rather than a deduction from geometric points.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, pp.202--203: the precise rank-one calculation required for the open-cell construction.

proof.text: For the determinant-one matrix group write $x(z)=I+zE_{12}$, $y(z)=I+zE_{21}$ and $d(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})$. On the open cell $x(u)d(t)y(v)$ define $\sigma=x'(u)d'(t)y'(v)$. For a product of two cell points, the inner pair $y(v)x(u_2)$ has $w=1+vu_2$. The bottom-right entry of the product is $t^{-1}w t_2^{-1}$, so the product is in this cell exactly when $w$ is a unit. The second Gauss formula of step 6 interchanges this pair. Moving the resulting diagonal past the outer root factors with the displayed torus-equivariance formulas and combining adjacent $x'$ and $y'$ gives exactly the cell coordinates of the matrix product. Therefore $\sigma$ is locally multiplicative and $\sigma(1)=1$. By [lem-sfb-sl2-open-cell-sheaf-extension] it extends uniquely to a homomorphism $F_{\mathrm{SL}}:\operatorname{SL}_2\to H$. The target is an fppf sheaf by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent], which also identifies the resulting natural transformation with a scheme morphism. Its restrictions are $x',y',d'$ and its Weyl value is $h$ by the last identity in step 6.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, pp.202--203: multiply on the explicit SL2 open cell, then use the existing open-cell extension lemma.

proof.text: In a local model $C\times J$, with $C$ a central split torus and $J$ one of SL2, PGL2, GL2, the map on $C$ is the specified $f_T|_C$. It commutes with $x'$ since the root character is trivial on $C$. It commutes with $h$ since $s_a$ fixes $C$, hence also with $y'$ and $d'$. Consequently it commutes with $F_{\mathrm{SL}}$: on the open cell this follows factor by factor, and uniqueness in [lem-sfb-sl2-open-cell-sheaf-extension] equates conjugation by each central-torus point with the original homomorphism. This constructs the product homomorphism for the SL2 model.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: remove and restore the central torus factor.

proof.text: For the PGL2 model, $\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{PGL}_2$ is an fppf cover: choose a GL2 representative locally in the quotient by scalar matrices and adjoin a square root of its determinant to normalize it. The extension adjoining a square root of a unit is finite free and faithfully flat, since its algebra has basis $1,z$ and $z$ is a unit. The kernel is $\mu_2$ inside the diagonal torus. On it $F_{\mathrm{SL}}=d'$ is trivial, since the corresponding diagonal scalar has trivial image in the PGL2 torus on which $f_T$ is given. Thus two lifts have equal images, and [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] descends $F_{\mathrm{SL}}$ to a homomorphism on PGL2. Its root values are $x',y'$. For the torus, a point of $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$ is, after a cover, the image of some $\operatorname{diag}(r,t)$; adjoining $z$ with $z^2=rt$, it is also the image of $\operatorname{diag}(r/z,z/r)=a^\vee(r/z)$, where the value is $d'(r/z)=f_T(a^\vee(r/z))$. Since $H(R)\to H(R')$ is injective for these covers by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent], the descended map equals $f_T$ on $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$. The central factor of step 8 is then restored.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: PGL2 reduction via the diagonal kernel, including characteristic 2.

proof.text: For the GL2 model, the map $\operatorname{SL}_2\times\mathbf G_m\to\operatorname{GL}_2$, $(M,z)\mapsto zM$, is an fppf cover by the same square-root-of-determinant construction. Its kernel consists of $(s^{-1}I,s)$ with $s^2=1$. Use the homomorphism $(M,z)\mapsto F_{\mathrm{SL}}(M)f_T(zI)$; its factors commute by step 8's argument for scalar matrices. On the kernel it has value $f_T(\operatorname{diag}(s^{-1},s))f_T(sI)=f_T(\operatorname{diag}(1,s^2))=1$. It therefore descends by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent]. On any diagonal $\operatorname{diag}(r,t)$, choose $z^2=rt$ and use $\operatorname{diag}(r,t)=z\operatorname{diag}(r/z,z/r)$; the value is $f_T(\operatorname{diag}(r,t))$. Thus the full torus restriction is the required one. Restore $C$ as before.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: the GL2 central product reduction with its diagonal kernel explicitly killed.

proof.text: The local homomorphisms on $K_a$ all have the same restrictions to $T$, $U_a$, and the section $n_a$. They consequently agree on $U_{-a}$, because conjugation by $n_a$ swaps the two roots, and hence on the open cell $U_{-a}TU_a$. The faithfully flat multiplication of two open cells in [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus], applied to the reductive pair $(K_a,T)$, implies equality on $K_a$ by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent]. This proves agreement over overlaps of the base cover and glues the local maps to $F_a:K_a\to H$. The group identities also glue. For $u\in U_{-a}$ the formula for the negative restriction is $f_N(n_a)f_a(n_a^{-1}un_a)f_N(n_a)^{-1}$, which is $g_{-a}$ by step 3; the positive restriction is $g_a=f_a$.

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4 proof, p.202: uniqueness and gluing of the rank-one maps, and their opposite-root restrictions.

proof.text: By definition $N_G(T)\cap K_a=N_{K_a}(T)$. The normalizer quotient for the rank-one pair $(K_a,T)$ in [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus] has Weyl group $\{1,s_a\}$, represented by $1,n_a$, and its kernel is $T$. Hence this normalizer is the disjoint union of $T$ and $n_aT$. On the first coset both $F_a$ and $f_N$ restrict to $f_T$, and on the second they have value $h_af_T(t)$. This proves the full required restriction on $N\cap K_a$, also on disconnected test algebras. When $\Phi$ is empty, there are no roots or simple centralizers to construct, so all conclusions indexed by them are vacuous. This finishes all clauses without changing the statement or imposing an additional hypothesis.
